Drug Delivery System Anisotropic Elasticity inherent to liquid crystals (LCs) allow micro-particles to be trapped within LCs without their coalesnce or diffusion into surrounding media.

By leveraging this elastic sequestration of microparticles and the stimuli-responsive properties of LCs, we have engineered a new class of smart LC materials that not only sense and optically report specific stimuli but also transform their surroundings by releasing the sequestered microcargo (e.g., drug, antibacterial agent).
For instance, we have developed the LC systems that can be activated by the touch of a human finger (temperature), introduction of chemical species, or the presence of motile bacteria.
Most significantly, this smart LC material represents the first example of the system that responds directly to living cells, analogous to the human immune system.

In this research project, we aim to explore how the self-reporting and self-regulating functions of the smart LC materials can be programmed through the interplay of intermolecular and interfacial forces in diverse geometries (NATURE, 557, 539 (2018)).
Cosmetics Liquid Crystals (LCs) have been widely used for Cosmetic applications due to their distinctive physicochemical properties and structural versatility.

Their biocompatibility and ability to form lamellar phases analogous to the lipid bilayers of the stratum corneum render them suitable carriers for bioactive compounds such as ceramides, peptides, and antioxidants.

The inherent elasticity of LCs facilitates the entrapment of functional molecules within the mesophase, allowing for sustained and localized delivery.
Furthermore, certain actives exhibit spontaneous self-assembly at the interface of LC droplets, contributing to enhanced stability and skin affinity.

Our research also investigates cholesteric LCs, which possess selective light-reflecting properties arising from their helical arrangement.
These optical characteristics enable their utilization in color cosmetics and UV-protective formulations.

Through systematic studies on phase behavior, molecular interactions, and interfacial phenomena, our laboratory aims to advance the development of functional and dermatologically compatible LC-based systems for cosmetic applications.

Bacteria We investigate fundamental properties of Motile Bacteria (e.g., chemo-taxis, collective behavior) and combine them with the unique features of LCs to design new class of smart materials, such as self-powered micro-robot, drug-delivery system, sensors.

Soft-Robotics Liquid Crystal Elastomers (LCEs) are rubber-like materials with the long-range molecular ordering so that reorientations of internal LC molecules enable the materials to shrink, expand, twist, or bend in a programmed way.
By patterning this alignment, therefore, LCEs can drive precise, reversible shape change in response to a certain stimuli (e.g., light, heat, chemical).

Building on this, we are designing new class of Soft-Robot by integrating LCEs with advanced molecular switches to realize (1) self-bending and self-twisting elements that generate propulsion (self-propelling actuators), (2) stimulus-guided modules that sense and pursue targets (self-tracking actuators), and (3) multifunctional grippers that capture, transport, or release payloads.
Importantly, these devices operate without embedded electronics, external power, or complex fabrication, enabling lightweight, wireless, and scalable actuation.

Sensors
Bio- & Chemical-Sensors We design Advanced Bio- & Chemical-Sensors by leveraging the unique properties of LCs that can translate nanoscopic and molecular-scale stimuli into macroscopic optical signals.

By collaborating with Korea government and industries (Samsung Electronics, COSMAX, and POSCO), we have been making significant advances in the design of Bio- & Chemical Sensors for identifying hydrogen gas, toxic gases, bacteria, viruses, biological molecules, interfacial phenomena, and intermolecular interactions.

Molecular Dynamics Simulation Molecular Dynamics (MD) Simulation is a computational method used to quantitatively analyze the structure, dynamics, and thermodynamics of molecular systems based on underlying physical models.
By employing MD simulations, we investigate how LC molecules interact with other chemical and biological species to uncover various intermolecular phenomena that emerge at the molecular scale.

Building on this knowledge, we aim to understand our experimental systems mediated by LCs and to design a new class of smart materials that can be used in diverse applications, including drug delivery and release systems, high-sensitivity sensors, soft actuators, microfluidics, and novel molecular/colloidal self-assembly platforms.
Self-Assembly We utilize the LCs as a soft template to synthesize nano- & micro-scale materials with a high level of control over size, organization, 3D structure, and functionality.

Ultrafast Dynamics Laboratory
What we do
Elucidating microscopic dynamics of prompt chemical and photophysical processes in condensed phases
Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave packets in Electronic Excited States
Development of New (and Old)
Time Domain Techniques
The goal of our research is to elucidate microscopic dynamics of prompt chemical and photophysical processes in condensed phases.

We put particular emphasis on the initial stages of the processes and the coupling between the electron and nuclear degrees of freedom, where the nuclear coordinates include both inter- and intra-molecular, as they play critical roles in most of the spectroscopy and determine the fate of a photoexcited system.

Our primary research tool is the femtosecond time-domain spectroscopy that can determine the structure and energy levels of a molecule directly while a molecule is undergoing chemical reactions and physical processes.

Depending on the system under scrutiny, a variety of femtosecond techniques including those developed in our own laboratory are employed; time-resolved fluorescence (TRF), 3 pulse photon echo peak shifts (3PEPS), spectrally resolved four wave mixing (SRFWM), transient grating (TG), tau-resolved transient grating (TRTG), and transient absorption (TA).
Summarized below are some of our recent results made possible by the state-of-the-art instruments developed in our laboratory.
Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text: When a molecule is excited impulsively by a short pulse of light, vibrational wave packets are created, which are manifested in the oscillations of the time trace in various time-resolved spectroscopies, TA being a typical example.

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text: The nature of the vibrational modes excited and their dynamics provide a wealth of information on the molecular dynamics, structures of the states involved, and the coupling between them.

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text:
In general, the coherent nuclear wave packet can be launched by any nuclear rearrangements occurring faster than roughly half of the vibrational period.
Excited state intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT) is one such example.

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text: Observation of the dynamics of the vibrational wave packet in the excited state can be done unambiguously by TRF as far as the time resolution is high enough.

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text: A TA signal may also give excited state dynamics through the stimulated emission component, although a TA signal may be complicated by the ground state bleach, excited state absorption, and product absorption.

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text: We have developed a noncollinear fluorescence upconversion technique that now gives near perfect time resolution with 20 fs pump pulses.

meta.heading: Creation and Detection of Vibrational Wave Packets in Electronic Excited States

text:
Development of New (and Old) Time domain Techniques
Time-resolved fluorescence (TRF)
We have developed the TRF technique to unprecedented time resolution of around 30 fs (FWHM) employing noncollinear sum frequency generation and a Cassegrainian pair as an imaging optic (Opt.
Lett.

30, 96-98 (2005); Opt.
Express 16, 20742 (2008)).
In addition, full emission spectra can be recorded without the conventional spectral reconstruction method.
The time delay, phase matching angle of the BBO crystal, monochromator are moved in unison to record the fluorescence spectra for a given time while compensating group velocity dispersion.

Tau (t) Resolved Transient Grating (TRTG)
Third order nonlinear spectroscopic techniques such as 3PEPS, TG, and TA give information on the dynamics of the system through the transition frequency correlation function of the probe, M(t).

Although they all more or less follow M(t), only the 3PEPS is background-free.
That is, 3PEPS is free from the population relaxation component to give M(t) directly including inhomogeneity.
However, it requires a long acquisition time due to the scanning of two time delays in 3PEPS.
We devised a nonlinear time domain scheme, electronic coherence period (denoted as t conventionally) resolved transient grating (TRTG), which provides M(t) with only a population delay scan.

TRTG is similar to TG except the electronic coherence period t is set to a finite value, usually a few femtosecond, and the third order signals at two phase matching directions are compared and subtracted.

TRTG was implemented based on a diffractive optics to set the t delay accurately within a few tens of attoseconds.
The significance of TRTG was verified by theoretical calculation as well as experiments for a dye in various solvents.
(Initial idea was published in J.
Chem.
Phys.
120, 5269-5274 (2004), and the full account is to be published).

Spectrally resolved four wave mixing (SRFWM)
Spectral dispersion of a four wave mixing signal has been reported before.

We have further developed the technique to a few cm⁻¹ precision in center frequency measurement, which enables us to resolve both the ground state and the excited state dynamics through the ground state bleach (GB) and excited state stimulated emission (ESE) components in a TG experiment, respectively.
As an example of SRFWM, detailed frequency-time resolved spectra of a dye molecule in methanol following impulsive excitation by 20 fs pulses is presented.

The transient spectra are successfully separated into the GB and ESE, and the center frequencies of each component are measured as a function of time delay, which allows the observation of the nuclear dynamics in each state separately.
Both GB and ESE show oscillations due to the vibrational wave packet motions in each state.

The ambiguity in the assignment of an oscillation to either the ground or the excited electronic states, which exists in all third order nonlinear time domain spectroscopies, can be resolved unambiguously in this SRFWM experiment.

More importantly, the solvation dynamics can be obtained from the time dependent blue shift of the ground state hole spectrum, which is purely due to the fluctuation of the solvent molecules around the probe in the ground state, and from the usual time dependent Stokes shift of the excited state particle spectrum, which is due to the dissipation of the probe in the excited state.

Development of the Light Sources
To perform those experiments for various chemical systems, it is essential to make our own femtosecond laser to meet the stringent requirements.

An ideal laser for femtosecond spectroscopies requires the wavelength tunability especially in the visible, high yet controllable pulse repetition rate, and moderate pulse energy for wavelength conversion by nonlinear processes.

A cavity-dumped Ti:sapphire laser meets those requirements except the limited wavelength tunability.
One way to get a wavelength tunability is to build a Ti:sapphire amplifier and an optical parametric amplifier, although that is not economic and the repetition rate is limited to a few kHz.

We have developed a cavity-dumped optical parametric oscillator based on a periodically poled lithium niobate (Opt.
Lett.
30, 1855-1857 (2005)).

A notable feature is to implement positive group velocity dispersion for much higher pulse energy, and many feed back mechanism including the cavity length and pump beam pointing to stabilize the OPO.
The output is enough for various nonlinear processes to efficiently convert the wavelength well into UV.

" The long-term goals of our group are to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of immune regulation and tolerance induction under healthy and diseased conditions and to develop novel immuno-modulatory for hyper-immune disorders.
"

TFs in Immune homeostasis
Roles of transcription factors in Immune Homeostasis
Identification of regulatory network in health and disease
Changes in gene transcription play a central role in regulating virtually all events from the development to the function of immune cells.

We are interested in studying the role of immune related transcription factors (TFs), such as Ets, NFAT and ID family members.
By using transgenic and conditional knockout mice, we aim to identify the functions of the TFs under homeostatic and disease conditions.
At a mechanistic level, we are also applying various genomic and proteomic approaches to elucidate the corresponding molecular mechanisms.

IL-10 Regulation
Mechanisms of IL-10 gene regulation in immune cells:

Role of cis-regulatory elements
Post full genome sequencing of the mice and human genome, the presence of Conserved Non-coding Sequences (CNS) between different species was identified for multiple genes.

Of them, we are interested in CNS-9, which is located 9kb upstream of the IL-10 transcription start site.
CNS-9 is a key cis-acting element of IL-10 regulation in various immune cells.

To determine the molecular mechanism, we are checking for gene looping between CNS-9 and other cis-regulatory elements, and are identifying proteins or regulatory DNA elements that bind to CNS-9.
To elucidate the functional importance of CNS-9 for IL-10, we have generated CNS-9 deficient mice.
We will utilize these mice to check the importance of CNS-9 for IL-10 expression in diverse immune cells in homeostatic and disease situations.

Role of Probiotics
Characterization of regulatory DCs and iTreg cells
induced by probiotics
The human gut is home to trillions of microorganisms, including 1000 species of bacteria, and are collectively termed the intestinal microbiota.

The microbiota is in constant interaction with the host and has various effects on the host, such as differentiation of immune cells i.e.
Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg) and T helper 17 cells (Th17).

Treg cells play important roles in suppressing inflammatory responses, especially in unwelcome situations such as autoimmune disease.
We are interested in elucidating how gut commensals like B.

bifidum, which colonize during early stage of life, induces Foxp3+ Treg cells, and aim to find the bacteria derived effector molecules involved in this process.
To fulfill our goal we use germ free and B.
bifidum monoassociated mice.
Our studies provide a mechanistic scenario of how gut commensal bacteria induce Treg cells, moreover, it also provides potential candidates for therapy of inflammatory immune disorders.

Gene delivery using biomedical polymer
Gene delivery is introducing nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA into target cells to correct defective genes which induce disease.
Generally, the correction is achieved through
1) introducing lacking genetic materials,
2) blocking mutated genes
3) replacing the mutated genes with normal genes

Our group has developed a variety of polymer based and hybrid gene delivery carrier utilizing cationic polymer, inorganic materials and even nucleic acids in order to protect the genes from enzymes or damages and facilitate uptake of the genes into the target cells.

Furthermore, various chemical bonds which could be cleaved at specific stimuli have been introduced for more effective gene delivery: pH, reducing environment and bio-molecules including ATP, sugar and nucleic acids have been applied.

As well, targeting moieties have been conjugated with the carrier for specific tumor-targeting.
Those strategies provide highly effective and specific gene delivery, and we have used the strategies for developing novel gene delivery carrier as our research goal.

Cancer immunotherapy using nanoparticle
Cancer immunotherapy (CIT), harnessing the immune system to induce the death of cancer cells or alter the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, has been extensively investigated due to its therapeutic potential.

Despite its promising potential, instability of immunomodulators, systemic adverse effect, and resulting insufficient immunogenicity remain as barriers.
Our major goal of research is to design of nanomaterial-based strategies that enhance the efficiency and efficacy of immunomodulators.

Introduction of nanomaterials into immumotherapy enables stable delivery of immunomodulators with spatiotemporal-specific release as well as combinatorial therapy with the existing cancer therapy methods including chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, and photodynamic therapy.

Recently, we are studying the site-specific immunomodulator delivery using tumor microenvironment and combination of immunotherapy with developed nanomedicine.
Our novel strategies would suggest new perspectives for breakthrough of current immunotherapy.

NO related materials
Nitric Oxide related materials
Nitric Oxide (NO)-related therapeutics is a rising research field, because NO has intrinsic physiological effects such as neurotransmitter, immune regulator and vasodilator etc.

However, due to the short life time of NO radical molecule, introducing NO donor is needed for delivering NO to human body.
Our group has applied various biocompatible NO donor for antibacterial effects, antitumor effects, vasodilation, wound healing effects and BBB opening effects.
Furthermore, stimuli responsive NO delivery system also has developed, such as ultrasound, high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) and pH to enhance therapeutic effect and reduce side effects.
However, if NO is overproduced by physiological disorders, it can lead to severe inflammatory diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and bowel disease etc.
For treating these disease, we also researches NO-responsiveness and try to extend NO-scavenging materials as therapeutics such as NO-responsive hydrogel and NO-scavenging nanogel.
We believed that our novel materials have a potential as a therapeutic material for various incurable and inflammatory disorders.

High programmability, predictability, and biocompatibility promise the DNA as an excellent biomaterial for biomedical applications.

Our Vision
The Nanotrio refers to a class of diverse nanomaterials developed at the intersection of nanophotonics, nanoplasmonics, and nanobiotechnology.

Our research explores the synthesis, characterization, and potential applications of nanomaterials, with a particular focus on quantum dots, plasmonic nanoparticles, and nanocomposites with tunable morphologies and sophisticated nanostructures.
We specialize in characterizing the “small world” of nanomaterials using absorption and emission spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, and zeta-potential analysis.
Through these analyses, we investigate the properties of synthesized materials and use the resulting insights to guide the future design of functional nanomaterials.

Our goal is to understand the unique physical properties of nanomaterials and translate them into practical applications in nanotherapy, nanoenergy, nanodiagnostics, and other emerging fields.
Ongoing Research Projects (For more information, please visit the Project page)
Our Nanotrio laboratory conducts research in nanoscience and nanobiology, focusing on the interaction between light and matter at the nanoscale.

We study the synthesis, surface control, assembly, and complexation of nanocrystals to develop nanostructures and advanced materials with potential applications in displays, photodetectors, photovoltaics, photoelectrochemical cells, sensors, and bioimaging.

In particular, we study semiconductor nanocrystals, such as quantum dots and QLED materials, as well as nanostructured materials based on gold nanoparticles that can be used for sensing and three-dimensional cell imaging.

By leveraging the unique physical properties of nanomaterials, we aim to develop functional materials for a wide range of optical, electronic, and biomedical applications.
We synthesize new nanocrystals by controlling precursor reactivity and reaction intermediates.
Quantum dots are inorganic nanocrystals with a molecular-level size distribution, and their small size allows a large number of atoms to reside at the surface.
For example, InP quantum dots, which are widely used in QLED displays, can contain approximately 1,000 to 10,000 atoms, depending on the size.

Although the exact atomic structure and growth mechanism of these nanocrystals remain difficult to determine, quantized intermediates can form during their synthesis.
These intermediates are structurally analogous to the critical nuclei described in classical nucleation theory.

Our research focuses on understanding these intermediate nanoclusters and controlling their formation through precursor chemistry, with the goal of establishing growth pathways and mechanistic principles for the development of high-performance QLED nanocrystals.

We also investigate surface chemistry at the nanoscale.
Surface chemistry is essential for forming efficient conjugates with proteins, DNA, and antibodies, and it plays a critical role in controlling colloidal stability and surface functionality.

In particular, we study ultrafast surface modification using quantized ions and investigate reversible surface bonding based on hydrogen-bonding interactions.
Through these approaches, we aim to establish precise and efficient strategies for tailoring nanocrystal surfaces.

Another major focus of our research is near-infrared optical materials.
Compared with conventional molecular or organic materials, quantum dots can emit in the near-infrared region while exhibiting high photostability and size-tunable optical properties.

Quantum-dot-based optical probes can also be miniaturized and used for ultrahigh-sensitivity sensing through solution-based processes such as inkjet printing.
Using these properties, we develop new near-infrared fluorescent probes and materials.

In addition, we are developing brain–computer interfaces that use autonomous quantum-dot probes to visualize real-time physiological signals in the brain, thereby enabling new approaches for understanding human cognition and neural activity.

We are also synthesizing biocompatible nanocrystals and converting them into oil-in-fluorocarbon materials for biomedical applications.
We develop nanorobotic probes that respond to environmental stimuli, such as pH, by changing their optical properties.
Like cuttlefish that change color in response to their surroundings, these nanorobotic probes are designed to alter their optical signals when exposed to specific environments.

Quantum-dot optical probes can also be used as next-generation display materials because they provide a wide color gamut and can respond sensitively to external stimuli.
By programming their response to specific conditions, these probes can visualize changes that are difficult to detect directly.

For example, quantum dots that respond to magnetic field variations are being investigated as magnetoplasmonic nanorobot probes that use gold nanoparticles and can be applied to next-generation transparent displays, including AR and VR technologies.
Finally, we are developing barcode technologies using near-infrared probes to overcome the limitations of conventional molecular probes and to enable simultaneous detection of multiple targets.

Because of their strong photostability, high brightness, and narrow emission bandwidth, quantum dots can provide highly multiplexed optical signals.
Antibody–quantum dot conjugates can be used for rapid and quantitative target detection in complex biological environments.
These nanomaterials offer advantages for medical diagnosis, bioimaging, and precision sensing by minimizing biological background interference and providing distinct multicolor optical signals.

Through this research, we aim to develop quantum-dot-based molecular barcode platforms capable of detecting multiple professional-level diagnostic signals simultaneously.

매직 크기 나노클러스터 합성
마직 크기 나노클러스터(MSC)는 분자 전구체와 콜로이드 양자점 사이의 중간 단계에 해당하는 나노 구조체입니다.

MSC는 수백 개 이하의 원자로 구성된 3 nm 미만의 극소 크기임에도 불구하고, 동일한 크기의 일반 나노입자보다 열역학적으로 높은 안정성을 나타내는 것이 가장 큰 특징입니다.
흡수 스펙트럼에서 특정 파장에 고정된 선명한 흡수 피크가 나타나는 것도 MSC를 구별하는 중요한 지표이며, 이러한 특성을 바탕으로 비고전적 합성 경로를 통해 다양한 나노소재를 제조하기 위한 전구체로서의 활용 가능성이 주목받고 있습니다.

본 연구팀은 MSC의 합성, 분리 및 물성 규명 연구를 수행하고 있으며, 나아가 MSC가 갖는 독특한 광학적 특성에도 주목하고 있습니다.
특히 정이십면체 구조를 갖는 MSC는 라세미 혼합물 형태로 존재하며, 리간드를 이용한 분리 또는 키랄 컬럼 크로마토그래피를 통해 좌우 거울상 이성질체로 분리될 수 있습니다.
이러한 키랄 MSC는 원편광이색성(CD) 스펙트럼에서 거울 대칭의 신호를 나타내는 등 특이한 광학 활성을 보이며, 이를 통해 MSC의 구조와 광특성 사이의 관계를 탐구하는 연구를 진행하고 있습니다.

과학기술정보통신부
양자점-고분자 복합 콜로이드 플랫폼을 활용한 바이오센싱 및 생체 이미징
양자점은 높은 광안정성과 조성에 따라 조절 가능한 발광 특성 덕분에 생체 환경에서의 신호 측정 및 이미징에 유망한 소재입니다.
본 연구팀은 양친매성 폴리에틸렌이민(amPEI)을 기반으로 수십 개의 양자점을 단일 나노입자 내에 캡슐화한 복합 콜로이드(QDCC) 플랫폼을 개발하고, 이를 다양한 바이오 응용으로 확장하는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.

복합 콜로이드의 외부에 고분자 전해질 다층막(layer-by-layer, LbL)을 순차적으로 코팅하면 구조적 견고성과 투과성을 세밀하게 조절할 수 있으며, 표면에 쯔비터이온 작용기를 도입함으로써 넓은 pH 범위와 고농도 염 조건에서도 우수한 콜로이드 안정성을 확보할 수 있습니다.
이를 기반으로 생체 내 표적 단백질에 대한 면역분석 시스템을 구축하고, 생물학적 자기조립을 통한 신호 증폭 전략을 적용하여 극미량의 바이오마커를 빠르게 검출하는 플랫폼으로 발전시키고 있습니다.

또한 amPEI의 유연한 내부 구조는 기체 분자가 쉽게 드나들 수 있어, 산화질소(NO)와 같은 생리활성 기체 분자에 반응하는 물질을 양자점과 함께 캡슐화하여 비율측정형(ratiometric) 센서로 활용하는 연구도 진행하고 있습니다.
이 플랫폼은 세포 내 산소 농도 모니터링, 산화질소 실시간 검출 등 다양한 생체 환경 측정에 적용 가능한 범용 나노센서 플랫폼으로 자리매김할 수 있을 것으로 기대됩니다.

자극 반응형 금 나노입자시스템

금 나노입자는 나노미터 크기에서 독특한 표면 플라즈몬 공명 특성을 나타내며, 입자 간 거리와 배열에 따라 광학적 특성이 크게 달라집니다.
본 연구팀은 금 나노입자의 표면에 외부 자극에 반응하는 리간드를 설계하여, pH 변화나 산화-환원 반응과 같은 화학적 신호에 의해 입자의 분산과 응집을 가역적으로 제어하는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.
리간드가 외부 자극에 반응하면 입자 간 상호작용과 플라즈모닉 커플링이 변화하고, 이에 따라 나노입자 집합체의 광학적 특성이 가역적으로 조절됩니다.

이러한 접근은 나노입자의 콜로이드 안정성, 조립 거동, 그리고 자극 의존적 광 반응을 정밀하게 제어할 수 있는 플랫폼을 제공합니다.
이를 기반으로 암 광열 치료, 광음향 이미징, 암세포 선택적 약물 전달 등 다양한 의생명 응용 연구를 진행하고 있습니다.
나아가 최근에는 전기화학적 자극에 의해 금속-리간드 배위 결합이 가역적으로 형성되고 끊어지는 현상을 활용하여, 입자 간 플라즈모닉 커플링을 전기적으로 제어하는 재구성 가능한 광학 소재 및 스마트 센싱 플랫폼 개발로 연구를 확장하고 있습니다.

나노결정 표면 화학 제어
나노결정의 성능은 내부 결정 구조만큼이나 표면에서 일어나는 원자 수준의 상호작용에 의해 결정됩니다.
본 연구팀은 은 칼코게나이드 나노결정을 중심으로, 표면 원자의 종류와 리간드 결합 환경이 나노결정의 광학적 특성과 화학적 안정성에 어떤 영향을 미치는지 체계적으로 연구하고 있습니다.
나노결정 표면에는 결정 격자 내부에 속한 원자와 격자 경계 바깥에 노출된 원자가 공존하며, 이 두 종류의 원자는 서로 다른 리간드 결합 특성을 나타냅니다.

본 연구팀은 이러한 표면 위치별 결합 특성의 차이를 규명하고, 이를 활용하여 나노결정을 안정적으로 패시베이션하는 전략을 개발하고 있습니다.
이를 통해 나노결정의 융합과 형태 변형 없이 양이온 교환이나 코어-껍질 구조 형성 같은 후속 화학 반응을 정밀하게 수행할 수 있습니다.
또한 표면에 존재하는 원자의 종류와 비율을 조절하면 나노결정 내 전하 트랩 특성을 원하는 방향으로 설계할 수 있다는 점에 주목하여, 이를 광검출 소자 등 실제 응용으로 연결하는 연구도 진행하고 있습니다.

양이온 교환을 통한 나노결정 조성 및 형태 제어
양이온 교환 반응은 음이온 격자를 유지한 채 양이온만을 선택적으로 치환하는 합성 전략입니다.
입자의 형태와 크기를 보존하면서도 조성을 자유롭게 바꿀 수 있어, 단일 전구체에서 다양한 합금 나노결정을 만들어내는 강력한 도구입니다.
본 연구팀은 전구체의 반응성을 정밀하게 설계함으로써 이 교환 반응의 경로를 원하는 단계에서 정확히 멈추는 방법을 개발하고 있습니다.

(1) 반응성 제어 전구체를 이용한 Ag-Au-S 양자점의 단계별 양이온 교환 기존 방법으로 Ag₂S 양자점에 금을 도입하면 조성이 불균일한 혼합물이 생성되어 발광 스펙트럼이 넓어지는 문제가 있었습니다.
본 연구에서는 금 전구체의 반응성을 리간드 배위, 금속 간 결합, 입체 효과를 통해 단계적으로 낮춤으로써, Ag₃AuS₂ 및 AgAuS 양자점을 높은 상순도로 선택적으로 합성하는 데 성공하였습니다.

이를 통해 적색~근적외선 영역(663–1192 nm)에 걸쳐 좁고 밝은 발광 특성을 구현하였으며, 전구체 반응성 설계가 합금 나노결정 합성의 핵심 원리임을 제시하였습니다.
(2) 형태 보존 양이온 교환을 통한 나노결정 설계 양이온 교환 반응에서 음이온 골격이 유지되는 특성을 활용하면, 입자의 형태와 구조적 특징을 그대로 보존하면서 조성만을 유연하게 바꿀 수 있습니다.

이 접근법은 두 가지 이상의 금속 성분을 포함하는 합금 나노구조체의 합성으로도 확장 가능하며, 기존 직접 합성으로는 구현하기 어려운 다양한 조성의 나노결정을 체계적으로 설계하는 플랫폼으로 활용됩니다.

이를 통해 색순도와 발광 효율이 동시에 우수한 청색 양자점 합성을 목표로 합니다.

Research Topics (KR)
진행 중인 연구 분야
● 나노트리오 연구실은 나노스케일에서 빛과 물질의 상호작용을 이해하고 제어하는 것을 목표로, 나노과학 및 나노바이오 분야의 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.

본 연구실은 나노결정의 합성, 표면 제어, 조립 및 복합화 연구를 통해 디스플레이, 광검출기, 태양전지, 광전기화학 소자, 센서, 바이오이미징 등 다양한 분야에 활용될 수 있는 나노구조체와 첨단 소재를 개발하고 있습니다.
특히 양자점 및 QLED 소재로 활용되는 반도체 나노결정과, 센싱 및 3차원 세포 이미징에 적용 가능한 금 나노입자 기반 나노구조체를 중점적으로 연구하고 있습니다.
이를 통해 나노소재 고유의 물리적 특성을 활용하여 광학, 전자, 바이오의학 분야에서 기능성 소재로 발전시키는 것을 목표로 합니다.

● 본 연구실은 전구체의 반응성과 반응 중간체를 제어함으로써 새로운 나노결정을 합성하는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.
양자점은 분자 수준의 크기 분포를 갖는 무기 나노결정으로, 매우 작은 크기 때문에 많은 수의 원자가 표면에 존재합니다.
예를 들어 QLED 디스플레이에 널리 사용되는 InP 양자점은 크기에 따라 약 1,000개에서 10,000개의 원자로 구성될 수 있습니다.
이러한 나노결정은 정확한 원자 구조와 성장 메커니즘을 규명하기 어렵지만, 합성 과정에서 양자화된 중간체가 형성될 수 있습니다.

이러한 중간체는 고전적 핵생성 이론에서 설명하는 임계핵과 구조적으로 유사한 나노클러스터로 볼 수 있습니다.
본 연구실은 이러한 중간 나노클러스터의 형성과 반응성을 이해하고, 전구체 화학을 통해 이를 제어함으로써 고성능 QLED 나노결정 개발을 위한 성장 경로와 성장 원리를 확립하고자 합니다.
● 또한 나노스케일에서의 표면화학을 연구하고 있습니다.
표면화학은 단백질, DNA, 항체 등과의 효율적인 결합체 형성에 필수적이며, 콜로이드 안정성과 표면 기능성을 조절하는 데 중요한 역할을 합니다.

특히 본 연구실은 양자화된 이온을 이용한 초고속 표면 개질과 수소결합 상호작용을 기반으로 한 가역적 표면 결합을 연구하고 있습니다.
이러한 접근을 통해 나노결정 표면을 정밀하고 효율적으로 조절할 수 있는 전략을 확립하고자 합니다.
● 다른 주요 연구 주제는 근적외선 광학 소재입니다.
일반적인 분자 또는 유기 소재와 비교할 때, 양자점은 높은 광안정성과 크기 조절이 가능한 광학 특성을 가지면서 근적외선 영역에서 발광할 수 있습니다.

또한 양자점 기반 광학 프로브는 소형화가 가능하고, 잉크젯 프린팅과 같은 용액 공정을 통해 초고감도 센싱 플랫폼으로 활용될 수 있습니다.
본 연구실은 이러한 특성을 활용하여 새로운 근적외선 형광 프로브와 소재를 개발하고 있습니다.
더 나아가, 자율적으로 작동하는 양자점 프로브를 통해 뇌의 생리적 신호를 실시간으로 시각화하고, 이를 기반으로 인간의 인지 및 신경 활동을 이해하기 위한 뇌-컴퓨터 인터페이스 기술을 개발하고 있습니다.

또한 생체적합성 나노결정을 합성하고 이를 오일-인-플루오로카본 소재로 전환하여 바이오의학 응용으로 확장하는 연구도 수행하고 있습니다.
● pH와 같은 환경 자극에 반응하여 광학 특성이 변화하는 나노로봇 프로브를 개발하고 있습니다.
주변 환경에 따라 색을 변화시키는 갑오징어처럼, 이러한 나노로봇 프로브는 특정 환경에 노출되었을 때 광학 신호가 변화하도록 설계됩니다.
양자점 기반 광학 프로브는 넓은 색 영역을 구현할 수 있고 외부 자극에 민감하게 반응할 수 있어 차세대 디스플레이 소재로도 활용될 수 있습니다.

특정 조건에 반응하도록 프로그래밍된 프로브는 직접 관찰하기 어려운 변화를 시각화할 수 있습니다.
예를 들어 자기장 변화에 반응하는 양자점은 금 나노입자를 이용한 자기-플라즈몬 나노로봇 프로브로 연구되고 있으며, AR/VR 기술과 같은 차세대 투명 디스플레이 응용으로 확장될 수 있습니다.
● 마지막으로, 기존 분자 프로브의 한계를 극복하고 여러 표적을 동시에 검출하기 위해 근적외선 프로브 기반 바코드 기술을 개발하고 있습니다.

양자점은 높은 광안정성, 강한 발광 세기, 좁은 발광 대역폭을 가지므로 다중화된 광학 신호를 제공할 수 있습니다.
항체–양자점 접합체는 복잡한 생물학적 환경에서도 표적을 빠르고 정량적으로 검출하는 데 활용될 수 있습니다.
이러한 나노소재는 생체 배경 신호의 간섭을 줄이고, 서로 구분 가능한 다색 광학 신호를 제공함으로써 의료 진단, 바이오이미징, 정밀 센싱 분야에서 장점을 가집니다.
본 연구실은 이러한 연구를 통해 여러 진단 신호를 동시에 검출할 수 있는 양자점 기반 분자 바코드 플랫폼을 개발하고자 합니다.

Nanophotonics
The emission wavelength and intensity of QDs can be precisely controlled, making them versatile materials for switchable probes in cellular and whole-body imaging, optical modulation, and light-emitting devices.
Our group synthesizes a wide range of nanomaterials, including core/shell QDs, nanorods, nanotetrapods, and nanoporous structures.

We have demonstrated the photomodulation of QD conjugates using additional UV excitation, which promotes electron transfer to the QDs and quenches their photoluminescence.
We have also developed inorganic-ligand-capped QDs as sensitizers for solar-cell applications.
1.

Optical properties of quantum dots
Semiconductor nanocrystals, commonly referred to as quantum dots (QDs), differ from bulk semiconductors in that their optical properties are strongly dependent on size.

In semiconductor nanocrystals with diameters of only a few nanometers, electrons and holes are confined within a space smaller than the exciton Bohr radius, giving rise to quantum confinement in all three dimensions.

This confinement produces discrete electronic energy levels and makes the band gap (BG) between the valence band and the conduction band dependent on nanocrystal size.
The BG determines the energy required for photoexcitation and the subsequent radiative relaxation process.

As the size of a QD decreases, the BG increases, leading to absorption and fluorescence at shorter wavelengths (Fig.
1).
QD core/shell structure can be classified into type-I and type-II (Fig.
2)

Semiconductor QDs can be categorized into type-I and type-II structures according to their band alignment.
In type-I QDs, the shell material has a larger BG than the core material, allowing the electron–hole pair to be confined within the core.

This confinement enhances photoluminescence (PL) efficiency, making type-I QDs useful for highly emissive applications.
In type-II QDs, the valence and conduction band edges of the core and shell are staggered, which spatially separates electrons and holes across the core/shell interface (Fig.
3a).

This charge separation makes type-II QDs attractive for energy-conversion applications, including solar cells.
Changes in the valence and conduction band alignment of the core and shell alter the spatial distribution of electron and hole densities.

This band engineering also creates an effective BG that is not determined solely by the intrinsic band gaps of the constituent materials, enabling control over both absorption and PL wavelengths (Fig.
3).
Colloidal nanocrystals synthesized from solution-phase precursors offer broad tunability in morphology and size, providing many opportunities for functional applications.

Morphological control is important because nanocrystal shape and internal structure influence electronic energy states, charge-carrier mobility, and exciton localization.
These morphologies can be controlled by regulating nucleation and growth processes from the atomic level.
Such processes are governed by both kinetic factors, including reactant concentration and diffusion, and thermodynamic factors, including surfactant concentration and reaction temperature.

Solution-based synthesis can produce highly crystalline nanocrystals with diverse shapes and offers notable advantages over conventional top-down methods.
We synthesize various types of nanocrystals, including core/shell QDs, nanorods, nanotetrapods, and nanoporous materials (Fig.
4a).

We have also reported supra-QDs (SQDs) (Fig.
4b), which are hierarchical superstructures composed of hundreds of individual QDs, each only a few nanometers in size, assembled through oriented attachment.

These SQDs may exhibit enhanced charge-carrier mobility and therefore show strong potential as sensitizers for solar-cell applications.
2.
Investigation of the properties of NPs induced by the incorporation of foreign atoms

Introducing foreign atoms into as-synthesized nanocrystals can alter their optical, electrical, and magnetic properties in addition to changing their composition.
Depending on the amount and distribution of the introduced species, this process can be classified in several ways.
One representative approach is doping, in which semiconductor nanocrystals are modified in a manner analogous to the doping of bulk semiconductors.

Doping is the intentional incorporation of foreign atoms into a pristine semiconductor host material to modulate its optical, electrical, and magnetic properties.
In bulk semiconductors, dopants ionize and provide additional electrons or holes depending on their valence states.

In the case of transition-metal dopants, the dopant spin can couple with the orbitals of the host material.
Because of these characteristics, doped semiconductors are widely used in semiconductor junction structures, including transistors and diodes.
In semiconductor nanocrystals, however, doping is strongly affected by quantum confinement and therefore produces behaviors distinct from those observed in bulk materials.
The confinement of excitons within an extremely small volume enhances their interaction with dopant ions, amplifying changes in optoelectronic and magnetic properties.

Doped nanocrystals therefore have potential applications in memory devices, photocatalysts, and bioimaging probes, in addition to conventional semiconductor junction structures.
Cation exchange is another method for introducing foreign atoms into a crystal lattice.
Because bonding in many semiconductor nanocrystals has substantial ionic character, newly introduced cations can replace original cations while preserving the anion framework.
This transformation enables the synthesis of sophisticated nanostructures, including metastable crystal phases and complex morphologies that are difficult to access through direct synthesis.
By controlling the amount of foreign ions, cation exchange can be used for doping, heterostructure formation, or the synthesis of entirely new materials.
The exchange reaction is driven by differences in the thermodynamic stability of the reactants and products, as well as by ligand-mediated complexation under specific reaction conditions.
The feasibility of a given exchange reaction can be evaluated by considering the reaction conditions, solubility products, and standard enthalpies of formation of the relevant materials (Fig 5).

In nanocrystals, even when the constituent materials are identical, the crystal structures obtained after cation exchange can differ depending on particle size because thermodynamic stability is size-dependent (Fig.
6).
Therefore, investigating how cation-exchange outcomes vary with nanocrystal size is important for understanding the reaction mechanism.

After cation exchange, optical spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and other atomic-level characterization methods should be used to confirm the composition and crystal structure of the final material.
3.
PL modulation of QD

The emission wavelength and intensity of QDs can be modulated, making them promising materials for switchable probes in cellular and whole-body imaging, optical modulation, and light-emitting devices.

We used quasi type-II QDs to develop photoluminescence-modulating probes that respond to external stimuli.
Charging quasi type-II QDs, in which electrons and holes are spatially separated, induces photoluminescence (PL) spectral switching.

The initial emission state can be recovered through a subsequent neutralization step.
Reversible PL switching over many repeated cycles was demonstrated by alternating UV excitation between on and off states (Fig.
7).
We also developed a modulation sensor based on a PL on/off system.

In addition, reversible and wavelength-selective PL modulation was investigated by controlling charge transfer between QDs and quenchers.
4.
QD-based Solar Cells
A solar cell (SC) converts light energy directly into electrical energy.

Although silicon SCs have been commercialized on a large scale, they remain costly and require complex fabrication processes.
Nanocrystal-based SCs offer a potentially simpler and more cost-effective alternative.

Several types of SCs use QDs, including QD-sensitized SCs, hybrid SCs composed of QDs and conducting polymers (Fig.
8), and Schottky-type SCs.
Although these SCs have different device architectures, they all rely on light absorption followed by charge generation, separation, and transport.

Charge separation and transfer are influenced by the morphology of the QDs and the structure of the active layer.
The use of QDs allows the absorption wavelength to be tuned, and their colloidal dispersibility in various solvents enables solution-processable device fabrication.
Therefore, QD-based SCs represent a promising research direction for developing low-cost solar-energy conversion technologies.
By identifying the conditions required for high power conversion efficiency, experimental studies can provide insights into simple and scalable fabrication strategies for QD-based SCs.

Nanoplasmonics
Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) arises when free electrons in metal nanoparticles collectively oscillate in resonance with incident electromagnetic energy at the interface between the metal and the surrounding dielectric medium.

Noble metal nanoparticles exhibit strong SPR when their dimensions are reduced to the nanoscale, and their optical properties can be precisely tuned by controlling the metal composition, particle size and shape, and local dielectric environment.
These tunable SPR characteristics make noble metal nanoparticles highly versatile platforms for spectroscopic analysis, optical imaging, sensing, and therapeutic applications.
Our group develops advanced metal nanoparticle complexes for highly efficient cancer therapy and photoacoustic-guided drug delivery.

Properties of Surface Plasmon Resonance
Conductive metals contain a high density of free electrons that are not strongly localized to individual atoms.

Because these electrons can collectively respond to external electromagnetic fields, metallic nanostructures can exhibit surface plasmon resonance (SPR) when their dimensions are reduced to the nanoscale.
SPR gives metal nanoparticles unique optical properties.

In particular, noble metal nanoparticles, such as gold and silver nanoparticles, interact strongly with visible light and exhibit intense absorption and scattering, with optical cross sections that are orders of magnitude larger than those of typical organic dyes.
They also show high resistance to oxidation and photobleaching, making them powerful optical probes that can complement or replace conventional organic fluorophores.

The optical responses of noble metal nanoparticles are highly tunable because their plasmon resonance can be controlled by the dielectric properties of the metal, as well as by the size, shape, and local environment of the nanostructure.

Our goal is to design and synthesize diverse metallic nanostructures and to investigate their optical properties using spectroscopic and imaging tools.
We further aim to apply these nanostructures to biological and biomedical systems (Fig.
1).

Dark-Field Microscopy
Dark-field microscopy (DFM) visualizes scattered light from a specimen, whereas conventional transmission-mode microscopy forms images using transmitted light.
Metal nanoparticles can generate strong contrast under DFM because they efficiently scatter incident light at wavelengths that match their SPR.

Because scattering signals from small metal nanoparticles are intense and highly sensitive to plasmonic properties, DFM enables optical visualization even at the single-particle level.
DFM is also useful for distinguishing materials that may show only weak contrast in conventional imaging modes.

This capability allows the SPR properties of individual metal nanoparticles to be characterized and enables biological imaging using metal nanoparticles as scattering-based contrast agents (Fig.
4).

Photoacoustic Imaging Using “Smart” Gold Nanoparticles
Photoacoustic imaging (PAI) is an emerging hybrid imaging modality that combines optical excitation with ultrasound detection.

As a nonionizing biomedical imaging method, PAI can provide molecular and functional information, including hemoglobin oxygen saturation, blood flow, and tissue morphology.
It is therefore well suited for biomedical studies, including the monitoring of tumor physiology and treatment responses.

In PAI, image contrast is determined by the optical absorption properties of the target.
Exogenous contrast agents with strong near-infrared (NIR) absorption can enhance PA signals because NIR light penetrates deeply into biological tissues.

“Smart” gold nanoparticles (SANs) can rapidly aggregate under mildly acidic conditions, which are commonly found in tumor microenvironments.
This aggregation induces a red shift in their absorption spectrum toward the red and NIR regions.

As a result, PA amplitude increases under mildly acidic conditions while remaining relatively unchanged at physiological pH.
By combining tumor accumulation with high PA conversion efficiency, SANs can significantly amplify PA signals in cell-level and small-animal experiments (Fig.
6).
These properties make SANs a promising platform for PA-guided drug delivery, enabling real-time identification of delivery targets and on-demand therapeutic administration.

Nanobiotechnology
QD-based optical probes provide a promising platform for in vivo bioimaging and next-generation medical imaging applications because of their bright luminescence, resistance to photobleaching, and size-tunable emission wavelengths.

Our group develops NIR-II-emitting QD probes and has demonstrated cancer diagnosis using QD–antibody conjugates.
We have also engineered amphiphilic polyethylenimine-derivative platforms that incorporate QDs for cell labeling, targeted delivery, gene delivery, and ratiometric oxygen sensing.
1.

Biological applications of Quantum dots
Semiconductor QDs present a possible new technology for in vivo bio-imaging and future medical-imaging applications.

QDs have proven potential as imaging contrast agents due to their bright luminescence, their resistance to photobleaching, and their tunable emission wavelengths.
The main impediment to the use of QDs for biological applications is their biocompatibility.
QDs that contain toxic elements such as Cd, Pb, Hg, or As have limited biological applications.

High quality ‘non-toxic’ QDs have been synthesized (e.g., InP, ZnTe/ZnSe, CuInS2; AgInS2); they are free from potential leakage of toxic heavy-metal ions, and photoluminesce at wavelengths that can be selected by adjusting the size of the QD.

The new methods of synthesizing ‘non-toxic’ QDs using various solvents and QD precursors have been investigated to obtain bright and photostable QDs that promise application to in vivo medical imaging.
2.
Surface modification, functionalization and bioconjugation of QDs for biological applications
QDs are synthesized in inorganic solvent to obtain high quality, so their surfaces should be modified for bioimaging applications.
The surface molecules for QDs should give good colloidal stabilities in aqueous solutions without aggregation, and should have appropriate sites to allow conjugation with biomolecules.
To be suitable for applications in targeted imaging or in long-term in vivo imaging, QDs must be colloidally stable and must have minimal non-specific binding.

QDs that have been modified to have zwitterionic surface molecules can maintain colloidal stability over broad ranges of pH and ionic strength, and to show minimal non-specific adsorptions (Fig.
1).

Moreover, the zwitterionic QD surface ligands can also be used in conjunction with other functional groups; this trait allows simple conjugations for highly specific targeting while retaining the advantages of a zwitterionic QD surface (Fig.
2).
3.
Cancer Diagnosis Using QD - Antibody Conjugates

Cancer is a very heterogeneous system.
Multiplexed QD imaging is well-suited to detecting such heterogeneous systems.
QDs are also bright, photostable, and allow multiplexing by a single excitation wavelength.
QDs have broad absorption profile with large one-photon and two-photon absorption cross sections, narrow and symmetric emission profile, and large effective Stokes shifts.

To improve the accuracy of cancer detection, multiple biological targets must be imaged concurrently; these advantages of QDs can be used in multiplexing to achieve fluorescence molecular imaging of cancer tissues.

Doctors frequently use endoscopy to detect colon cancer, but the diagnosis is based on the clinician's naked-eye perception, which is subjective and error-prone.We developed a rapid and accurate molecular fluorescence imaging technique that uses antibody (Ab)-coated QDs (Ab-QDs) that are sprayed and washed simultaneously on colon tumor tissues inside live animals, then excited and imaged by endoscopy.
QDs were conjugated to matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 9, MMP 14, or carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) Abs with zwitterionic surface coating to reduce nonspecific bindings.

The Ab-QD probes can diagnose tumors on sectioned mouse tissues, in fresh mouse colons stained ex vivo and in vivo, and in fresh human colon adenoma tissues in 30 min and can be imaged to a depth of 100 μm.

The probes successfully detected not only cancers that are readily discernible to the naked eye, but also hyperplasia and adenoma regions.
Sum and cross-signal operations provided post-processed images that can show complementary information or regions of high priority (Fig.
3).

This multiplexed QD, spray-and-wash, and endoscopy approach provides a significant advantage for detecting small or flat tumors that may be missed by conventional endoscopic examinations and bestows a strategy for the improvement of cancer diagnosis.
4.
NIR-II emitting QD probes

The NIR biological window from 650 nm to 1700 nm allows deeper penetration than visible light into biological tissues such as skin and blood, because these tissues scatter and absorb less light at long wavelengths than at short wavelengths.

The window between 650 nm and 950 nm (NIR-I) has been exploited extensively for in vivo optical imaging of live animals, but little research has considered use of the longer-wavelength window (NIR-II) from 1000 to 1700 nm for in vivo fluorescence imaging of live animals.

Light scattering and absorption by biomolecules are much weaker in the NIR-II region than in NIR-I, so tissue penetration depth and spatial resolution are increased, and autofluorescence is decreased in NIR-II.

QDs can be advantageous fluorescent probes for molecular imaging in both the NIR-I and the NIR-II region.
CdTeSe, and CuInS2 have been developed as fluorophores in NIR-I, and have shown high photostability and quantum yield (QY) > 50%.

PbS and Ag2S QDs have been developed for NIR-II fluorescence imaging applications, and showed QY > 10% with inorganic shells in the aqueous phase (Fig.
4).
We report an enzyme-activatable NIR-II probe that exhibits fluorescence (FL) upon matrix metalloprotease activity in tumor microenvironment.
Bright and stable PbS/CdS/ZnS core/shell/shell QDs were synthesized as a model NIR-II fluorophore, and activatable modulators were attached to exploit photoexcited electron transfer (PET) quenching.

The quasi-type-II QD band alignment allowed rapid and effective FL modulations with a compact surface ligand modulator that contains methylene blue PET quencher.
The modulator was optimized to afford full enzyme accessibility and high activation signal surge when the enzyme was active.

In a colon-cancer mouse model, the probe demonstrated selective FL activation at tumor sites with tripled signal strength in 10 min (Fig.
5).

Sensing molecule by using QDs
Amphiphilic polyethyleneimine derivatives (amPEIs) were synthesized and used to encapsulate dozens of QDs.

The QD-amPEI composite was ~100 nm in hydrodynamic diameter and had an outer surface with a slight positive charge that is well suited for cellular internalization.
The outer positive surface was further exploited for gene delivery and targeting.

Co-delivery of QDs and GFP-silencing RNAs was demonstrated by attaching siRNAs to the outer surface; the process achieved transfection efficiency that was an order of magnitude higher than conventional gene transfections.

Hyaluronic acids were tethered onto the QD-amPEI for cell-specific targeted labeling, which achieved a specific-to-nonspecific signal ratio > 100.
The inside hydrophobic compartment was further applied to cohost oxygen-sensing phosphorescence Ru dyes along with QDs.

The ratiometric PL signals of the QD-Ru-amPEI oxygen probe show accurate and reversible oxygen-sensing capability and were successfully applied to cellular and spheroid models (Fig.
6).

Open-Vocabulary Scene Understanding
Open-vocabulary scene understanding reflects a paradigm shift away from recognition systems built around a small, fixed set of predefined categories.

Classical segmentation and detection models can only recognize the specific classes they were trained on — a "chair" model has no way to name or localize a "stool" if that word was never in its label set.

Open-vocabulary perception instead couples visual recognition with language, letting a model segment, ground, and reason about an arbitrary object category described in natural language at test time, whether or not that category ever appeared in training.

Active Perception
Active perception is grounded in a paradigm shift that computer vision underwent as it moved beyond passive, all-at-once scene analysis.

Rather than treating a camera or a model as a fixed device that must take in an entire scene and try to make sense of everything it sees, active perception treats the observer as something that can choose — where to look, how to move through and interact with a scene, or which view to prioritize — in order to answer a specific question as efficiently as possible.
Embodied AI & Language-Driven Robot Manipulation

The lab's embodied AI line investigates why end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle with long-horizon manipulation, and proposes a modular approach centered on open-vocabulary affordance grounding rather than mapping instructions directly to low-level actions.

The core hypothesis is that manipulation becomes tractable when it is decomposed into intermediate, physically grounded representations — where on an object a task-relevant region is, how a hand should contact it, and how the whole body should move to get there — rather than learned as one opaque instruction-to-action mapping.

This is a deliberate move away from black-box, end-to-end learning toward a more analytical and explicit formulation of manipulation, where each intermediate representation can be inspected, interpreted, and reasoned about on its own terms.

Scene Graphs & Human-Centric Scene Parsing
Understanding a visual scene often requires more than naming the objects in it — it requires parsing the scene into a structured representation of entities and the relationships between them.
A scene graph makes this explicit: nodes for objects, edges for their relationships, turning an image into a graph rather than a flat list of detections.

When the entities being related are people — interacting with objects, forming groups, or simply needing to be perceived accurately in the first place — this general scene-parsing problem becomes human-centric, and the lab's work in this space treats human-object interaction, group and social behavior, and even pose perception as specialized instances of the same underlying graph-parsing challenge.

Symmetry Analysis & Equivariant Learning
Many visual patterns aren't arbitrary — they're structured by symmetry: an object looks the same after a reflection, a rotation, or some other transformation.

Building models that can detect this structure, or that inherently respect it, is a distinct research problem from ordinary recognition, because standard convolutional and attention architectures have no built-in notion of "this feature should transform predictably when the input does." The lab has a sustained line of work addressing this gap from two complementary angles: finding where symmetry exists in an image or shape, and building network architectures that are structurally equivariant to transformations like rotation and reflection by design.
Actions, Events & Long-Horizon Reasoning from Videos

meta.heading: Actions, Events & Long-Horizon Reasoning from Videos

text: Beyond recognizing what is in a single frame, video understanding requires reasoning about how content unfolds over time — segmenting a stream into meaningful units, anticipating what comes next, locating precise moments of change, answering questions that require following a narrative, and tracking specific objects reliably as they move and occlude.

meta.heading: Actions, Events & Long-Horizon Reasoning from Videos

text: The lab has a sustained program across all of these temporal reasoning problems, and a defining trend across the group's recent work is treating generative modeling — diffusion in particular — and large language models not as end tasks in themselves, but as flexible backbones for representing and reasoning about temporal structure.

meta.heading: Actions, Events & Long-Horizon Reasoning from Videos

text: Relational Representation Learning for Video Understanding

meta.heading: Relational Representation Learning for Video Understanding

text: Before a system can reason about actions, events, or long video narratives, it first needs a way to represent motion itself — and for a long stretch of the lab's history, that representation problem was treated as unsolved rather than assumed.

meta.heading: Relational Representation Learning for Video Understanding

text: Standard video architectures apply spatio-temporal convolution or attention uniformly across space and time, treating motion as something that emerges implicitly from stacked appearance features.

meta.heading: Relational Representation Learning for Video Understanding

text: This line of the lab's research instead argues that motion has its own structure — correspondence and relation between neighboring regions across time — and that structure should be modeled explicitly rather than left to convolution or attention to discover on its own.

meta.heading: Relational Representation Learning for Video Understanding

text: Visual Correspondence & Geometric Matching

Finding reliable correspondences between images, shapes, and point clouds is one of the lab's longest-running research threads, tracing back over a decade to early work on semantic correspondence with object proposals and continuing through today's group-equivariant formulations.

The core problem is deceptively simple to state — given two visual observations of related content, which parts correspond to which?
— but solving it robustly across viewpoint change, intra-class variation, symmetry, and partial observability has proven to be a deep and recurring research challenge.

Our research interests are 1) drought mechanisms, risk, and predictability, 2) large-scale land surface modeling focusing on the land cover and use change impact, 3) river and reservoir monitoring via remote senesing and unmanned vehicles, and 4) socio-hydrology with a focus on the dynamics of social response during water-related disasters.

Group Motto:
"We are committed to maintaining integrity in our scholarly products, ownership of our intellectual properties, citizenship of our group, and diversity in our community.
"

We strive to increase society's resilience to natural disasters through an integrative understanding of social-natural systems.
The natural hazards we study include drought, heatwave, wildfire, flood, earthquake, and compound extremes.

Our analyses span various spatiotemporal scales, ranging from catchment- to global-level and sub-seasonal to decadal timescales.
Our approach is interdisciplinary converging hydrology, climatology, hydraulics, and social psychology.

We hope this will advance our understanding of the coupled dynamics between social and natural systems.
We always keep an eye out for new research collaboration opportunities.

Understanding social behavior and response to water-related disasters
Big data have hidden, but meaningful, information about our society's behavior and response to influential events.

For example, water-related disasters, such as drought and flood, cause rapid increase in public awareness/interest when they happen.
Despite the skillful prediction, lack of timely social response to these disaster exacerbates their adverse effects including fatalities and economic losses.

To transform our society to a water-related disaster-ready environment, better understanding of social dynamics (potential triggers and growth and decay patterns of public interest/awareness) is warranted.
Lately, big data from information search activities in the cyberspace provide high-resolution records with the unprecedented sample size.

Our research group aims to advance the current knowledge of not only the current prediction skill but also the social response during the emergency of natural/human disasters related to water resources.

Topic 01

Metal halide perovskite semiconductors have demonstrated outstanding performance in optoelectronic devices such as solar cells, LEDs, and transistors, thanks to their excellent properties and ease of processing.

In particular, they offer new possibilities for implementing CMOS circuits through low-cost, low-temperature processes, addressing the growing demand for high-mobility p-type semiconductors.
View More
Topic 02

P-type Metal Oxide Semiconductors
P-type metal oxide semiconductors have emerged as materials of significant interest in the low-power electronics industry due to their good stability and low off-state current.
Their potential applications span a wide array of technologies, including transistors, transparent electronics, display systems, and photovoltaic devices.

However, in contrast to the superior electrical performance of n-type metal oxides, the involvement of the oxygen 2p orbital in p-type counterparts leads to localization of the valence band maximum (VBM).
This electronic characteristic results in reduced hole mobility within p-type semiconductors.

Our research is dedicated to enhancing hole mobility and optimizing the on/off current ratio in p-type materials to overcome these limitations.
View More
Topic 03
Two-Dimensional Layered Semiconductors

2D semiconductors exhibit unique characteristics that make them highly promising for next-generation electronic devices.
With atomically thin layers, they enable excellent gate control even at ultra-short channel lengths, supporting continued transistor miniaturization.

Their dangling-bond-free surfaces minimize interface trap states, allowing for high carrier mobility and low contact resistance, essential for improved device performance.
Additionally, 2D semiconductors offer tunable electronic properties, such as adjustable bandgaps depending on layer thickness.

Our research focuses on their potential for integration into flexible electronics, low-power devices, and 3D monolithic structures, highlight 2D semiconductors as a transformative material for future semiconductor technology.

Metal Halide Perovskite

Semiconductors
Two-Dimensional Layered
Semiconductors

The past two decades have witnessed the enormous success of metal halide perovskite semiconductors in various optoelectronic devices, like solar cells, LEDs, and most recently transistors, due to an ideal set of optoelectronic properties and processing capability.

In particular, considering the urgent demand for high-mobility p-type semiconductors, metal halide perovskite provides a new opportunity to create CMOS circuits in a low-temperature and cost-effective way.

Despite certain performance improvements that have been achieved through material design, film processing, and device engineering, a critical understanding of the key properties and potential of these emerging materials for transistor application remains lacking.

Therefore, we intend to develop halide perovskite semiconductors for high performance p-type thin-film transistors for commercialization.
This project mainly studies the topics below but not limited to this.

Fuel Cell
A fuel cell uses the chemical energy of hydrogen or another fuel to cleanly and efficiently produce electricity.
If hydrogen is the fuel, electricity, water, and heat are the only products.
Fuel cells are unique in terms of the variety of their potential applications; they can provide power for systems as large as a utility power station and as small as a laptop computer.

Fuel cells can operate at higher efficiencies than combustion engines, and can convert the chemical energy in the fuel to electrical energy with efficiencies of up to 60%.
Fuel cells have lower emissions than combustion engines.

Hydrogen fuel cells emit only water, so there are no carbon dioxide emissions and no air pollutants that create smog and cause health problems at the point of operation.
Also, fuel cells are quiet during operation as they have fewer moving parts.

Battery
Recent development of Electrical vehicles, and portable devices requires high capacity and energy density batteries.
Many other researches were conducted to develop electrical performance of the batteries.
Such as doping, electrode surface modification and etc.

However closer research in atomic and electronic scale research was barely accomplished.
Our group closely investigate the structural or electrical phenomenon, utilizing PLS(Pohang Light Source).
We expect this research will provide fundamental understanding of battery performance in atomic scale and further development of high capacity and energy density energy.

Water Electrolysis
Water electrolysis(also called water splitting) is the decomposition of water into oxygen and hydrogen gas due to the passage of an electric current.
This technique can be used to make hydrogen gas, a main component of hydrogen fuel, and breathable oxygen gas.

It ideally requires a potential difference of 1.23 V to split water.
However, real water electrolyzers require higher voltages for the reaction to proceed.
The part that exceeds 1.23 V is called overpotential, and represents any kind of loss and nonideality in the electrochemical process.
Electrocatalysts can facilitate this reaction.

Carbon dioxide is an abundant potential carbon resource on Earth, and it is also a greenhouse gas whose atmospheric concentration has increased sharply over the past two centuries Chemical fixation of carbon dioxide (CO2) is an attractive technique for utilization of carbon resources, as well as for the reduction of the atmospheric concentration of CO2.

Carbon dioxide is a potential carbon resource abundant on earth.
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 is the conversion of carbon dioxide to more reduced chemical species.

The first examples of electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide are from the 19th century, when carbon dioxide was reduced to carbon monoxide using a zinc cathode.
Research in this field intensified in the 1980s following the oil embargoes of the 1970s.

CO2 can be removed by the reduction that produces various chemicals, such as carbon monoxide (CO), methanol (CH3OH), methane (CH4), and formic acid (HCOOH).
In our lab, we are mainly focused on the CO2 reduction to CO using various metallic catalysts.

Anti-corrosion
In modern times, with the development of stainless steel, the corrosion resistance of steel has improved dramatically.

However, corrosion in extreme conditions such as cryogenic, high temperatures, abrasion and seawater environments still causes economical loss and environmental damage and has become a major cause of safety issues.
Since it is almost impossible to replace and repair corrosion parts in such a harsh environment, the need for structural materials with strong corrosion resistance is increasing day by day.
Our group is exploring ways to improve the anti-corrosion properties of structural materials without losing mechanical properties via alloy composition control or surface treatment.

Battery Recycling
In order to meet global target of carbon emission, automotive industries are radically changing.
Millions of electric vehicles are now on roads, consequently, tones of end-of-life batteries will come out after decades.

In comparison to the number of end-of-life batteries and market size of battery recycling industries in the near future, the development of technology is still lag behind and the players in this field are not enough.

Thus, our group set our sight on developing advanced battery recycling technology using hydrometallurgical processes.
Battery recycling technology definitely will occupy highly demanding part in battery industries.

Research Topic 3 : Renewable energy with Process Simulation and LCA/TEA
Research Goal (연구 목표): 재생에너지 기반 공정모사를 통한 친환경 에너지 기술의 실현 가능성 및 지속가능성 평가 플랫폼 개발

Our research goal is to develop a systematic evaluation and design framework for renewable energy technologies by integrating process simulation with life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA).

This framework aims to assess the environmental and economic feasibility of renewable energy production processes, including electricity- and hydrogen-based systems, as well as emerging clean energy technologies.

In particular, our research focuses on (i) the development and assessment of environmentally friendly processes for renewable energy production, (ii) the design and evaluation of perovskite solar cell (PSC) fabrication and recycling processes using biomass-derived green solvents, and (iii) the modeling, analysis, and optimization of carbon capture and utilization (CCU) pathways based on CO₂ reduction potential and economic performance.

LAB introduction
1.
Metabolic engineering
In metabolic engineering, enhanced production of value-added chemicals requires precise flux control between growth-essential competing and production pathways, and optimized precursor balance.

By engineering genetically tractable strains using these metabolic engineering strategies, efficient conversion of biomass into bioactive compounds, biofuels, and bioplastics can be achieved.
-Escherichia coli

Escherichia coli has been widely regarded as a genetically tractable strain due to its well-characterized genetics, the availability of a wide range of molecular tools, and its high transformation efficiency.
-Vibrio sp.dhg

Brown macroalgae are emerging as a sustainable alternative feedstock with the potential to alleviate concerns about competition for food resources and the limitations of conventional agricultural cultivation.
However, about 50% of the carbon components of brown macroalgae are composed of alginate.

Most conventional microorganisms cannot metabolize alginate without additional pretreatment, limiting its use as a feedstock.
In MDSB lab, we isolated and characterized a fast-growing, alginate-utilizing microorganism, named Vibrio sp.
dhg.

In contrast to Vibrio natriegens, this strain is capable of robust growth with alginate as the sole carbon source.
It has emerged as a promising platform for the efficient conversion of brown macroalgae sugars into diverse value-added biochemicals.
Lim et al., Nat.
Commun, 2019

-Bacillus,Pseudomonas, and etc.
They are also being engineered, and other novel strains are being identified.
2.
Synthetic Biology
Synthetic biology is a emerging research field to redesign and construct the biological parts, devices, and systems for useful and practical purpose.

We are currently developing new molecular tools, and applying these cutting-edge technologies to design and construct high performance microorganism (mainly Escherichia coli, and Vibrio sp.dhg) for the production of biofuels, commodity chemicals, and bioactive compounds including pharmaceutical proteins from renewable biomass.

1) Fine-tunable and predictable expression level control system
- UTR Designer
: It is a computational tool that predicts and designs the mRNA translation initiation region to modulate translation efficiency in prokaryotes.
↑
Click!
Seo SW, Yang JS et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2013

- Repressor library
The repressor library can be constructed by varying the expression levels of the repressor, based on degenerate 5′ UTR sequence variants generated by UTR Library Designer.

Modular application of the repressor library enables fine regulation of the flux between the target product biosynthetic pathway and growth-related pathway, thereby enhancing the production of a diverse range of target chemicals.
JY Lee, S Cha, et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2021

2) Enzyme activity engineering based on sequence co-evolution analysis
- sequence co-evolutionary analysis to control the efficiency of enzyme reactions (SCANEER)
: It uses A.A.
sequence information as input to find activity-enhancing mutations in distal site from the active site of the enzyme based on sequence co-evolution analysis.

By excluding mutations that are likely to cause loss of function of the enzyme, SCANEER facilitates the identification of variants with improved enzymatic activity.
Based on the results of SCANEER analysis, we can design high quality library for enzyme engineering.

Kim et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2022
3) Design and Characterization of Biosensors for the high-throughput screening
- RNA-based Biosensor & Protein-based Biosensor

: To engineer an enzyme in the metabolic pathway, the method should be able to associate the enzyme activity with the production of target metabolites, as the ultimate goal of modifying the enzyme in the biosynthetic pathway is to improve metabolite production.

In addition, isolation of positive mutants from libraries is the most critical part for directed evolution of enzymes.
For these reasons, genetically encoded biosensors composed of biomolecules recognizing metabolites have been proposed and developed.

A biosensor is a biological device that detects specific molecules and converts the detection into a measurable signal, like fluorescence intensity or growth-coupled response.
By using biosensors, high-throughput screening of metabolite producing microorganisms can be achieved.

This approach provides the simple and efficient tool to engineer the pathway enzymes in metabolic engineering.
Seok JY et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2018

Flow Physics and Engineering Lab

기계공학과
Flow physics; Propulsion; Turbomachinery; Renewable energy; AI for mechanics; Quantum CFD

Fluid Dynamics & Numerical Analysis
We investigate a wide range of flow phenomena—flow separation and wakes around complex geometries, fluid–structure interaction (FSI), and multiphase flows—using high-fidelity numerical methods including direct numerical simulation (DNS).

Our goal is to uncover the underlying physical mechanisms and to predict these phenomena with high accuracy.
HPC / GPU Computing
Media coming soon

We leverage massively parallel computing and GPU acceleration to run high-resolution flow simulations on grids of hundreds of millions of cells at high speed.
By maximizing computational efficiency and scalability, we enable analyses of large-scale problems that were previously out of reach.

Turbulence & Transition Control
We control the laminar-to-turbulent transition process and near-wall flow separation through active and passive techniques.

By designing and validating control strategies, we target the performance gains required in real-world applications, such as drag reduction and flow stabilization.
Design & Optimization of Aero and Power-Generation Gas Turbines

We characterize the internal flow and combustion of gas turbines used in aircraft propulsion and power generation through precise numerical analysis.
Based on these results, we optimize blade geometry and operating conditions to improve efficiency and stability.

Reinforcement-Learning (AI) Control of Wind-Turbine Pitch and Yaw
We apply reinforcement-learning (AI)-based control to optimize wind-turbine blade pitch and yaw angles in real time.
The goal is to maximize power output while reducing structural loads, even under fluctuating wind conditions.

Optimal Design of the Porous Transport Layer (PTL) for Hydrogen Fuel-Cell Vehicles
We optimize the microstructure of the porous transport layer (PTL), a key component of hydrogen fuel-cell electric vehicles.
By improving mass and heat transport, we enhance fuel-cell efficiency and durability.

Turbulence Prediction
Prediction
Ground Truth
We predict the spatiotemporal evolution of turbulent flow fields using neural-network–based models.
Prediction results are compared with ground-truth simulations to verify the model’s accuracy and reliability.
Optimal Analysis & Design

We introduce machine learning to accelerate flow analysis and efficiently explore large design spaces, substantially reducing computational cost while deriving optimal designs.
Turbulence Modeling

We develop data-driven, neural-network–based turbulence models to overcome the limitations of conventional models, aiming for reliable turbulence analysis with improved predictive accuracy and generalization across diverse flow conditions.
Quantum-Native Numerical Algorithms

Time evolution of the simulated flow field (t = 1–6)
Evolution of three-dimensional vortical structures

We develop fluid-dynamics numerical algorithms optimized for the characteristics of quantum computing hardware, targeting quantum acceleration of large-scale flow problems that are intractable for classical computing.

We quantitatively analyze how the noise inherent in today’s quantum hardware affects the accuracy of numerical results, and study analysis techniques that remain reliable in noisy environments.

Variational quantum circuit for quantum machine learning: data encoding, entangling and variational layers, and measurement-based optimization

We apply quantum machine learning to fluid-dynamics problems to explore new analysis and prediction methodologies, aiming for a next generation of computational fluid dynamics that combines quantum computing with data-driven approaches.
